comment.value: The reviewers’ scores were A, BA, and BA, indicating overall support with some concerns. Strengths include the novelty of releasing the first publicly available wrist bone instance segmentation dataset with SvdH scoring, expert annotations across multiple institutions, and thorough benchmarking with released code and splits. Limitations noted were the relatively small size, demographic homogeneity, class imbalance, lack of annotation reliability reporting, limited benchmarking robustness, and the restricted external validation cohort, as well as the absence of recent foundation models and a blinded benchmark setup. These issues were addressed in the rebuttal with clarifications, added analyses, and commitments to improvement. Ethical concerns, mainly around data representativeness, imaging variability, and deployment readiness, should be explicitly clarified in the final version. Given its value and the authors’ thorough responses, I recommend acceptance, with the expectation that these improvements will be included in the camera-ready paper.

## Response to Reviewer jEcC:
Thank you for recognizing the clinical importance of the wrist region and the unique value of RAM-W600 as the first multi-institutional dataset providing both segmentation and scoring for RA diagnosis. We appreciate your positive remarks on the dataset’s annotation rigor, task design, and comprehensive coverage of clinically meaningful joints. We would like to express our sincere gratitude for your valuable and constructive feedback.

### 1. Limited Demographic Diversity
At present, there are no publicly available hand X-ray datasets specifically focused on RA. Due to ethical review constraints, we are only permitted to release data from a limited number of approved institutions. Unfortunately, all RA data that received approval for release are from Japan. We acknowledge this limitation and will explicitly state it in the revised manuscript.

To mitigate the potential bias caused by a single-region dataset, we incorporated publicly available non-RA data and provided corresponding instance segmentation masks of the carpal bones. In addition to the non-RA cases included at the time of submission (73 cases from the USA [1]), we have added 12 new cases from Bangladesh [2], 47 new cases from China [3], and 116 new cases from Japan (6 cases from Hokkaido University (HU) and 110 cases from Hokkaido Medical Center for Rheumatic Diseases (HMCRD)). Please refer to the repo on Huggingface for detailed information. We hope this will help reduce the impact of geographic and demographic homogeneity and strengthen the dataset’s generalizability.

[1] Gertych A, et al. Bone age assessment of children using a digital hand atlas. Comput Med Imaging Graph, 2007, 31(4–5): 322–331.

[2] Abedeen I, et al. FracAtlas: A dataset for fracture classification, localization and segmentation of musculoskeletal radiographs. Sci Data, 2023, 10: 521.

[3] Yao S, et al. A radiograph dataset for the classification, localization, and segmentation of primary bone tumors. Sci Data, 2025, 12: 88.

### 2. Severe Class Imbalance
Please refer to our response to the second comment from Reviewer e5eA for a detailed explanation.

### 3. No Annotation Reliability or Uncertainty Analysis
Our annotation team consists of a radiological technologist and 2 clinically experienced experts, including a board-certified radiologist with over 25 years of experience and an orthopedic doctor with more than 5 years of clinical practice. Their expertise ensures that the annotations are both medically accurate and clinically relevant.

For segmentation tasks, initial annotations were created by a radiological technologist and subsequently verified by the radiologist. For classification tasks, three annotators independently labeled the data, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion and consensus.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and will include this information in a revised version of the manuscript to clarify the annotation process and its reliability.

### 4. Lack of Statistical Robustness in Benchmarking

### 5. Limited Utility of External Validation Set
In response, we have expanded our dataset by incorporating additional non-RA cases, including 12 new cases from Bangladesh [1], 42 new cases from China [2], and 58 new cases from Japan (3 cases from Hokkaido University (HU) and 55 cases from Hokkaido Medical Center for Rheumatic Diseases (HMCRD)). As a result, the non-RA portion of the dataset now includes 185 cases. The age distribution of these cases has a mean of 37.2 years and a standard deviation of 19.7 years, which contributes to a more balanced and diverse population. Please refer to the repo on Huggingface for detailed information.

We hope this expansion improves the utility and representativeness of the dataset for broader clinical research applications.

### 6. Absense of State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Foundation Models in Benchmark

### 7. No Public Leaderboard or Blinded Test Evaluation
At present, the entire dataset, including the test set, is fully open to the community. 
This decision was made to promote transparency and accessibility during the initial release. Currently, we do not have the resources to construct a separate hidden test set, but we acknowledge the importance of robust benchmarking and plan to consider building a blinded evaluation platform in the future.

We also note that several widely used medical imaging datasets do not provide leaderboards or blind test evaluations, such as BTXRD [1] and MURA [2]. Nevertheless, they continue to serve as valuable benchmarks for the research community. In this spirit, we aim to maximize the utility of our dataset by encouraging broad participation and reproducibility while exploring future options for more formalized evaluation.

## Response to Reviewer e5eA:
Thank you for recognizing RAM-W600 as the first public multi-task dataset for wrist RA in CR (X-ray), combining expert-annotated segmentation and SvdH BE scoring across diverse sources. We appreciate your acknowledgment of its clinical value, annotation difficulty, and potential to advance RA CAD and wrist disorder research.

### 1. Most RA cases are from a single geographic region (Japan) and a relatively homogeneous ethnic group, which could limit generalizability.
Thank you for your comment regarding the geographic and ethnic composition of the RA cases. Please refer to our response to the first comment from Reviewer jEcC for a detailed explanation.

### 2. High BE scores are rare, so training robust models for advanced disease progression is challenging.
Thank you for pointing out the challenge associated with the rarity of high BE scores. We would like to offer the following clarifications:

1. Long-tail distributions are common in medical classification tasks, especially in chronic disease assessment. This challenge is inherent to the task and cannot be easily resolved by simply expanding the dataset. Our goal is to construct a dataset that faithfully reflects the realities of clinical data rather than artificially balancing it.

2. The long-tailed nature of SvdH scores in RA is clinically grounded. With advances in medical care, early detection and effective use of disease-modifying treatments have drastically reduced the number of patients progressing to late-stage RA over the past two decades. As a result, high BE scores have become increasingly rare in modern cohorts. We will clarify this point in the revised manuscript to emphasize the clinical factors underlying the long-tailed distribution.

3. CR imaging is typically used for monitoring RA progression, especially during the early and moderate stages where treatment adjustments are still possible. Once the disease reaches an advanced stage, CR imaging is no longer considered essential for progression tracking, and as a result, radiographs are often not acquired in late-stage clinical practice.

Taken together, we view the observed imbalance not as a limitation of the dataset, but as a critical and realistic challenge intrinsic to the task.

### 3. Bone overlap and subtle erosive changes still cause significant boundary errors for SOTA models.
Thank you for highlighting the issue of boundary errors caused by bone overlap and subtle erosive changes. We agree that these factors remain highly challenging, even for SOTA models and we have mentioned this in the Visualization part of Section 4.1 (Page 7).

However, rather than being a limitation of our method, we consider this to be an inherent difficulty of the task itself. One of the main goals of our work is to address these specific challenges, which are representative of the clinical complexity involved in wrist radiograph analysis.

### 4. Other modalities like CT or MRI could offer more 3D structural detail for wrist joints but are not included.
Thank you for the suggestion regarding the use of other imaging modalities such as CT or MRI. While these modalities can indeed provide more 3D structural detail, our target is specifically X-ray imaging. 
X-rays are the most widely used modality in clinical practice for diagnosing wrist conditions due to their accessibility, cost-effectiveness, and established diagnostic value. The purpose of our work is to build a dedicated X-ray dataset and develop models tailored to this setting, rather than pursuing a multimodal approach.

## Response to Reviewer 5gdV:
Thank you for recognizing RAM-W600 as the first dataset dedicated to wrist bone instance segmentation and its value for future RA research. We appreciate your positive comments on the thorough benchmarking and the dataset’s potential to advance RA-related applications.

### 1. The dataset size is limited. The dataset includes only 621 radiographs from 227 patients across four medical centers. For a 2D dataset, this scale is relatively small and may limit the generalizability of the findings.
Thank you for raising the point about dataset size. While our dataset includes 621 radiographs from 227 patients, we would like to emphasize that the annotation process for this task is extremely complex and resource-intensive, requiring expert-level interpretation of fine-grained joint-level features across 14 anatomical regions per image (already described in the 3rd paragraph of the Introduction, Page 2). Notably, we also annotated the overlapping regions between carpal bones, which is rarely addressed in existing datasets and significantly increases the annotation burden.

Compared to other publicly available datasets in this domain, our dataset is already among the largest in terms of both image count and annotation granularity. We encourage reference to Table 1 in the manuscript, which provides a detailed comparison with existing datasets. In addition, we appreciate your suggestion and have expanded our dataset by incorporating data from 2 external datasets (BTXRD [1] and FracAtlas [2]) and one internal dataset, adding 426 new images (175 images with segmentation annotation and 251 images with SvdH BE score annotation). Please refer to the repo on Huggingface for detailed information.

[1] Yao, S., et al. A Radiograph Dataset for the Classification, Localization, and Segmentation of Primary Bone Tumors. Sci Data 12, 88 (2025).

[2] Abedeen, et al. FracAtlas: A Dataset for Fracture Classification, Localization and Segmentation of Musculoskeletal Radiographs. Sci Data 10, 521 (2023).

### 2. Class Imbalance in BE Scores. As acknowledged by the authors, the dataset is imbalanced, with most patients exhibiting low BE scores. This skew may hinder the model's ability to generalize to cases with severe erosion.
Thank you for pointing out the class imbalance in BE scores. Please refer to our response to the second comment from Reviewer jEcC for a detailed explanation.

### 3. The paper does not clearly explain how the evaluation is conducted for BE versus non-BE regions, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the reported results.

Thank you for pointing this out. We apologize for not clearly explaining the evaluation procedure for BE versus Non-BE regions in the manuscript.

In our segmentation baselines, the distinction between BE and Non-BE regions is based on the SvdH BE score. Specifically, if the total BE score for a radiograph is greater than 0, we consider the image to contain a BE region. This rule is used to stratify cases into BE and Non-BE groups for evaluating segmentation performance.

For the classification task, we perform joint-surface-wise BE classification, focusing on the six joint surfaces of clinical interest. A joint surface is labeled as BE if its corresponding SvdH BE score is greater than 0.

We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion and will include a clearer explanation of this evaluation procedure in a revised version of the manuscript.

### 4. Annotation quality control. The wrist region, particularly in areas with overlapping bones and erosion, is challenging to annotate. However, the paper lacks details on how annotation quality and consistency were ensured.
Thank you for pointing out the class imbalance in BE scores. Please refer to our response to the third comment from Reviewer jEcC for a detailed explanation.

### 5. How do population differences between the internal and external cohorts impact the evaluation outcomes? For instance, the external cohorts are notably younger—does this suggest that the evaluation includes easier cases, potentially leading to overly optimistic performance results? In the evaluation, the authors use data from three institutions for training and reserve the fourth for external evaluation. However, the age and gender distributions in the external cohort differ notably from those in the training data. A more balanced and representative split between training and evaluation sets would be preferable to ensure a fairer assessment of model generalizability.

Thank you for the thoughtful question regarding population differences between internal and external cohorts. In our evaluation, we did not explicitly separate samples by data source. Instead, all results are stratified by BE and NonBE categories, regardless of whether the images come from internal or external cohorts. This information is also summarized in Appendix Table 7, which provides the population breakdown by source.

Although the external cohort primarily consists of younger, healthy individuals, the evaluation setup does not rely on or benefit from this difference. Since both BE and NonBE cases are present in both internal and external cohorts, and the evaluation is strictly stratified by disease status, the potential bias raised in the question does not apply in our setting. To assess the impact of bone erosion more directly, we encourage reference to the BE-stratified performance table (see Table 4 on page 7), which evaluates model behavior based on disease status rather than data origin.

We also appreciate the comment regarding institutional differences between training and evaluation data. To clarify, we did not restrict evaluation to a specific institution. Both internal and external data were included in the evaluation phase without distinction. The external dataset was not used as a dedicated hold-out set but rather incorporated to enhance the diversity and demographic balance of the full dataset. This approach was intended to ensure broader coverage of patient populations and imaging conditions, thereby supporting more robust and representative model development.

summary.value: The paper presents RAM-W600, a new, publicly available, multi-institutional wrist radiograph dataset specifically tailored for research in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) computer-aided diagnosis (CAD). RAM-W600 uniquely provides two primary supervised tasks: (1) wrist bone instance segmentation and (2) Sharp/van der Heijde (SvdH) bone erosion (BE) scoring. The dataset consists of 621 posteroanterior (PA) wrist radiographs from 227 patients (154 RA, 73 non-RA), acquired from four centers. Out of these, 443 images include expert-verified pixel-level bone segmentation masks, and 548 images are annotated with SvdH BE scores across six joint regions. All images and annotations are released with code and a benchmark suite. Baseline segmentation models (Unet, DeepLabV3+, TransUNet, SwinUMamba, etc.) and BE classifiers (ResNet, MobileNet, MedMamba, etc.) are comprehensively benchmarked. The authors emphasize dataset curation rigor (anatomical complexity, expert annotation, class imbalance), extensive comparisons to existing datasets, and reproducibility. Despite strong technical efforts, limitations in demographic diversity, severe class imbalance (few severe BE cases), and unresolved challenges in boundary segmentation and subtle lesion detection are acknowledged. The paper positions RAM-W600 as a foundational resource for reproducible, rigorous RA CAD research, but some claims about generalizability and benchmark sufficiency appear premature.

strengths_contributions.value:
The RAM-W600 dataset stands out as a significant and timely contribution to the field of medical imaging and computer-aided diagnosis for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), specifically targeting the wrist. This region is clinically crucial yet underrepresented in existing public resources. The most notable strength of the work lies in its scope and ambition: RAM-W600 is the first publicly available, multi-institutional dataset providing both high-quality, expert-verified pixel-level wrist bone segmentation masks and Sharp/van der Heijde (SvdH) bone erosion (BE) scores on the same conventional radiographs. This dual-task focus enables rigorous evaluation of both anatomical segmentation and disease grading, which are fundamental for developing robust RA CAD tools. The dataset comprises 621 radiographs from 227 patients across four different centers, ensuring diversity in acquisition conditions, and is accompanied by a comprehensive set of baseline experiments and open-source code, which strongly supports reproducibility and benchmarking.

A key contribution is the careful curation and annotation pipeline: 443 images are annotated with pixel-level instance segmentation for 14 wrist bones, while 548 images are scored for BE in six clinically meaningful joint regions, all conducted under the supervision of senior radiologists. The dataset documentation is exemplary, with clear task definitions, transparent description of data splits, and a well-structured file organization (Sections 3 and A). Extensive tables and figures compare the RAM-W600 to all major existing datasets (Tables 1–3), establishing its novelty and superiority in terms of coverage, annotation quality, and public accessibility. The paper is well-organized, clearly written, and includes highly informative figures and tables (e.g., Figs. 1–3, 6, and 9; Tables 4–5, 7–11) that illustrate not only the dataset statistics and composition but also highlight the inherent challenges of the tasks, such as class imbalance and bone overlap.

Moreover, the authors situate their contribution thoughtfully within the context of prior work, explicitly noting the limitations of existing datasets (which typically offer either segmentation or scoring, but not both, and are often not public) and highlighting how RAM-W600 overcomes these gaps. The open release of data, code, and detailed annotation formats (including example scripts and file structures) significantly lowers the barrier for other researchers to develop, compare, and fairly evaluate new algorithms in this domain. In sum, RAM-W600’s combination of clinical relevance, multi-task design, annotation rigor, and open science ethos make it a highly valuable resource for the medical imaging and AI community, with strong potential to drive progress in reproducible, impactful RA research.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Despite its significant contributions, the RAM-W600 dataset exhibits several important limitations that constrain its immediate impact and generalizability. First, as acknowledged by the authors in the Conclusions and Limitations section (Section 5, p. 9), the demographic diversity of the dataset is limited: (1) All RA cases are derived from a single geographic region and relatively homogeneous ethnic population, raising concerns about the robustness of models trained on RAM-W600 when applied to different clinical environments. (2) Second, the distribution of SvdH BE scores is highly imbalanced, with the overwhelming majority of joints assigned a score of 0 and only a handful of cases reflecting more severe erosive changes (as shown in Table 7 and Fig. 2C, pp. 6, 20). This class imbalance directly impacts the difficulty of both model training and fair benchmarking, particularly for detecting early-stage or severe RA, and is reflected in the limited sensitivity and low F1-scores reported for the BE classification task (Table 5, Fig. 10). While the authors mention these issues, the manuscript does not provide concrete strategies for mitigating class imbalance (e.g., resampling, synthetic augmentation, or focused annotation of rare cases), nor does it offer protocols for robust out-of-distribution validation.

Additionally, the work lacks a quantitative assessment of annotation uncertainty or inter-rater reliability, both for segmentation and BE scoring. This is an important omission, especially given the inherent subjectivity of radiological interpretation and the acknowledged challenges of expert annotation (Section 3.1, p. 5; Section 2, p. 2). The absence of error bars or variance measures in the reported benchmarks (Checklist, p. 15) further limits confidence in the reproducibility and stability of the published results, as all metrics are derived from single-seed runs. The external validation cohort is also limited in utility: it consists solely of young, healthy controls (mean age \~18, DHA cohort), which may not provide a realistic test of model generalization to non-RA or atypical RA populations (Section 3.2, p. 6; Fig. 2B).

On the technical side, the current set of baseline models, while broad, does not include several state-of-the-art foundation or promptable models such as SAM or DINOv2, which are now widely considered the standard in medical segmentation; their inclusion would significantly strengthen the benchmark and clarify the field’s true state of the art (Section 4.1, p. 6–7). Finally, the lack of a public leaderboard or blinded evaluation server raises the risk of test set overfitting and limits the dataset’s utility as a lasting benchmark (Section 4, implementation details). To address these issues, the authors should consider: (1) broadening demographic representation through additional data collection or external partnerships, (2) publishing annotation disagreement/uncertainty metrics, (3) reporting benchmark results with error bars or multiple random seeds, (4) including strong recent foundation models as baselines, and (5) establishing a public leaderboard or hidden test set for future community-driven benchmarking. These steps would greatly improve the dataset’s rigor, generalizability, and long-term value to the field.



---

### Summary

* **Limited Demographic Diversity**

  * All RA cases are sourced from a single region and relatively homogeneous population, restricting generalizability to broader clinical settings.
  * *Reference: Section 5, p. 9 (Conclusions and Limitations)*

* **Severe Class Imbalance**

  * The distribution of SvdH BE scores is highly skewed—most cases are labeled as score 0, with very few advanced cases represented (Table 7, Fig. 2C).
  * This makes it difficult for models to learn or benchmark performance on rare or severe cases, as reflected in the low sensitivity and F1-scores for BE classification (Table 5, Fig. 10).

* **No Annotation Reliability or Uncertainty Analysis**

  * The paper does not report inter-rater reliability, disagreement rates, or uncertainty measures for either segmentation or BE scores.
  * *Reference: Section 3.1, p. 5; Section 2, p. 2*

* **Lack of Statistical Robustness in Benchmarking**

  * All benchmark results are reported from a single random seed; there are no error bars or results from multiple runs, limiting the reliability of the reported metrics.
  * *Reference: Checklist, p. 15*

* **Limited Utility of External Validation Set**

  * The external (DHA) validation cohort consists mainly of healthy young controls (mean age \~18), which does not realistically reflect the diversity or pathology encountered in real clinical practice.
  * *Reference: Section 3.2, Fig. 2B*

* **Absence of State-of-the-Art (SOTA) Foundation Models in Benchmark**

  * The benchmark does not include strong recent models such as SAM or DINOv2, which are widely regarded as SOTA in medical segmentation.
  * *Reference: Section 4.1, pp. 6–7*

* **No Public Leaderboard or Blinded Test Evaluation**

  * The current test set is fully open, raising concerns of overfitting and limiting the dataset’s utility as a long-term, community-wide benchmark.
  * *Reference: Section 4 (Implementation Details)*

* **Suggestions for Improvement**

  * Broaden demographic representation, publish annotation disagreement and uncertainty measures, report performance with error bars or multiple seeds, include SOTA foundation models in the benchmark, and establish a public leaderboard or hidden test set.

---

* The RAM-W600 dataset fills a significant gap in publicly available resources for rheumatoid arthritis research, especially regarding multi-task evaluation on wrist radiographs. The comprehensive annotation and clear documentation are greatly appreciated.

summary.value:
This paper introduces RAM-W600, the first large-scale multi-task wrist dataset for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) assessment using conventional radiography (CR).
It combines:

Pixel-level wrist bone segmentation masks for 14 wrist bones

Sharp/van der Heijde (SvdH) bone erosion (BE) scores for key joint regions.

The dataset includes 621 wrist X-rays from 227 patients across multiple centers, plus comprehensive benchmarks on segmentation and BE scoring tasks using various deep learning models. The dataset and benchmark code are publicly available on GitHub and Hugging Face.

strengths_contributions.value:
First multi-task dataset for wrist RA in CR: Covers both instance segmentation and SvdH BE scoring — no comparable public dataset exists for the wrist with this level of detail.

Provided by experts, despite the wrist’s anatomical complexity and overlapping bones, which makes labeling challenging.

Images come from multiple hospitals and one external atlas, adding variation in acquisition conditions.

Evaluates multiple strong segmentation models (e.g., U-Net, SwinUMamba, TransUNet) and classification models for BE scoring, with detailed metrics.

Code, dataset, splits, and instructions are all publicly released.

The dataset supports research on RA CAD tools, bone erosion detection, joint space narrowing, and could be extended to other wrist-related disorders.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
Most RA cases are from a single geographic region (Japan) and a relatively homogeneous ethnic group, which could limit generalizability.

High BE scores are rare, so training robust models for advanced disease progression is challenging.

Bone overlap and subtle erosive changes still cause significant boundary errors for SOTA models.

Other modalities like CT or MRI could offer more 3D structural detail for wrist joints but are not included.

summary.value: This paper introduces a radiograph dataset, RAM-W600, for the assessment of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The contributions include: (1) annotations for the wrist region, which often presents severe bone overlapping and erosive changes; and (2) benchmark results for bone segmentation and bone erosion (BE) scoring tasks. This dataset opens new avenues for the development of advanced algorithms for RA assessment and may help improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical relevance.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This is the first publicly available dataset dedicated to wrist bone instance segmentation, providing a valuable resource for future research in RA assessment.

2. The authors conduct thorough benchmarking on two key tasks and demonstrate promising performance, highlighting the dataset's potential for advancing RA-related applications.

3. Code and datasets are made public.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The dataset size is limited. The dataset includes only 621 radiographs from 227 patients across four medical centers. For a 2D dataset, this scale is relatively small and may limit the generalizability of the findings.

2. Class Imbalance in BE Scores. As acknowledged by the authors, the dataset is imbalanced, with most patients exhibiting low BE scores. This skew may hinder the model's ability to generalize to cases with severe erosion.

3. The paper does not clearly explain how the evaluation is conducted for BE versus non-BE regions, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the reported results.

4. Annotation quality control. The wrist region, particularly in areas with overlapping bones and erosion, is challenging to annotate. However, the paper lacks details on how annotation quality and consistency were ensured.

5. How do population differences between the internal and external cohorts impact the evaluation outcomes? For instance, the external cohorts are notably younger—does this suggest that the evaluation includes easier cases, potentially leading to overly optimistic performance results?

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: In the evaluation, the authors use data from three institutions for training and reserve the fourth for external evaluation. However, the age and gender distributions in the external cohort differ notably from those in the training data. A more balanced and representative split between training and evaluation sets would be preferable to ensure a fairer assessment of model generalizability.

final_justification.value: The authors address the majority of my concerns, so I would like to raise my rating from 3 to 4.

title.value: RAM-W600: A Multi-Task Wrist Dataset and Benchmark for Rheumatoid Arthritis

abstract.value:
Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common autoimmune disease that has been the focus of research in computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) and disease monitoring. In clinical settings, conventional radiography (CR) is widely used for the screening and evaluation of RA due to its low cost and accessibility. The wrist is a critical region for the diagnosis of RA. However, CAD research in this area remains limited, primarily due to the challenges in acquiring high-quality instance-level annotations. (i) The wrist comprises numerous small bones with narrow joint spaces, complex structures, and frequent overlaps, requiring detailed anatomical knowledge for accurate annotation. (ii) Disease progression in RA often leads to osteophyte, bone erosion (BE), and even bony ankylosis, which alter bone morphology and increase annotation difficulty, necessitating expertise in rheumatology.
This work presents a multi-task dataset for wrist bone in CR, including two tasks: (i) wrist bone instance segmentation and (ii) Sharp/van der Heijde (SvdH) BE scoring, which is the first public resource for wrist bone instance segmentation. This dataset comprises 1048 wrist conventional radiographs of 388 patients from six medical centers, with pixel-level instance segmentation annotations for 618 images and SvdH BE scores for 800 images. This dataset can potentially support a wide range of research tasks related to RA, including joint space narrowing (JSN) progression quantification, BE detection, bone deformity evaluation, and osteophyte detection. It may also be applied to other wrist-related tasks, such as carpal bone fracture localization.
We hope this dataset will significantly lower the barrier to research on wrist RA and accelerate progress in CAD research within the RA-related domain.
